utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the members of the Prosecution, the members of the Defence teams. We are in the same composition today as on the previous days. For the record, we don't need to waste time in having the appearances. Before beginning, I must apologise for the delay, but I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to say that an organisation involves all parties in an orderly relationship with the view to achieving a certain objective. I said that is what I thought, because I noticed that on the intranet, yesterday's hearing was announced as a closed session hearing, when, in fact, it was a public hearing. Today I verified to see that the time announced for the beginning hearing was 10.30, rather than 9.30, as we had decided. Therefore, I should ask the registrar to pay attention to these matters. Otherwise, we will not achieve the goals that we have set ourselves. In fact, I believe that each one of us has to assume his responsibilities and do his part of the work. The President of the Chamber should not have to check and review these things to ensure the proper functioning of the proceedings. Everyone must assume his share of the responsibility. So the delay today is partly due to this confusion because the beginning was announced for 10.30 instead of 9.30, and as a rule, our hearings will always begin at 9.30, going on until 2.30, except when an exception is made. That is the rule. And all exceptions will have to be announced with sufficient time in advance. We respect the time of other people, and therefore I draw the attention of the registrar to these matters so that the necessary corrections can be made. So now we can continue with the testimony of Mr. Kvocka, and I therefore give the floor to Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Simic: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we started yesterday with a discussion on your first contacts with the Omarska Investigation Centre, and we will continue on that same subject. You said explicitly yesterday that after the Omarska police station department or, rather, its personnel had taken over the security duties from members of the police whom you didn't know, that you recognised three or four bodies, and you showed us where they were on the grass opposite the restaurant in the administration building. Do you have any knowledge as to whether among those bodies was the body of the late Mr. Anhil Dedic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, people said that one of those killed was he. This was talked about among the guards, who, in the meantime, had established contact with some of the prisoners, and they probably heard that from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not personally know Mr. Anhil Dedic, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't verify because you didn't approach the bodies either, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the knowledge you have about the death of the late Dedic was obtained from others who told you that he was killed when attempting to escape.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was what was said some seven or eight days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, upon your first arrival in the Omarska Investigation Centre, what were you wearing? Did you have a uniform on or something else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wearing my regular police uniform, which was worn for many years in the course of -- during the former Yugoslavia and the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a standard uniform that was worn for the past five, six months or more?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than that, for longer than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any insignia on your uniform that would indicate any measure of superiority?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All policemen had the same insignia on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a difference when it came to the uniform worn by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have on you on that occasion, and was it in any way different from the standard weapon that you were issued?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was armed with a standard weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that standard weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were never issued an automatic rifle when entering the Omarska Investigation Centre.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign up for one, like all active duty policemen, but I didn't carry it on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was usually in the premises of the police, and sometimes in the official vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard yesterday from you that you were a highly disciplined policeman. In the course of your career, did you ever violate the rules regarding the way in which you wore your uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the rules envisage the obligation to wear gloves, especially those gloves without fingers that we know from police films?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not envisaged by the rules, nor was it allowed for policemen to wear any such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever use such gloves in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your stay in Omarska, did you notice that any policeman wore such gloves?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were some who used such gloves but not among the active-duty professional policemen. Not a single one of them did I notice wearing them. Anyway, there were only two or three of us active-duty policemen in Omarska at the time, so I can assert that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of anyone who you saw wearing such gloves because, after all, those were unnatural times.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one person with the same surname as mine, and his name is Milojica, so his name is Milojica Kvocka, I think that occasionally I did see saw him wearing such gloves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Meakic as the commander of police department? Did he react when he saw that? As you said yourself, that that was not in line with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that Mr. Meakic arrived some 15 minutes after the group or maybe at the same time as the group. What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dressed in the same way as I was, wearing the standard police uniform that was worn at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Meakic have as weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same weapon as all active-duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own a rifle called pumperica? Did such a rifle appear in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never had possession of such a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did such a rifle -- was it seen in Omarska at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see one in the parts of the compound where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That first day, whether it was the 27th to the 28th or the 28th to the 29th of May 1992, you said that food was not provided for the detainees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. No mention was made of food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Meakic inform you and the other guards what was the plan regarding food?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the first day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards have food provided for that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Meakic take any steps to find, as donors, one of the well-known businessmen to get some food on that first day for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on that first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he contact Mr. Andzic in connection with such matters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that when we go on to the next day. I'm talking about the first day now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Your Honour, we've been quite patient in regard to leading questions and questions which introduce facts which are not in evidence, but now that we're in Omarska itself, we would object to the continuing leading nature of the questions that are being asked. For example, the last question was: "When did" -- first he said: "Did Mr. Meakic take any steps to find one of the well-known businessmen to get some food on the first day for the detainees?" That, we would allow as a lead-in, but the next question: "And when did he contact Mr. Andzic?" That's a fact that is not in evidence. It is a leading question. We would ask that for Omarska, at least, counsel allow the witness to testify and he refrain from these kinds of questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, do you have any reaction to this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the objection and I shall pay closer attention to the wording of my questions, but I thought that we had covered most of these questions together with Mr. Keegan in the interview with Mr. Kvocka. So these things are something that the Prosecution is familiar with. I had no intention to lead, and I shall try and be more specific in my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Put non-leading questions to the witness so that the witness can testify properly. Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Thank you, Ms. Hollis, for your objection and remark. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that first day, were members of the security replaced by new persons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening there was a change of shift. The entire personnel was replaced and that is when I also went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought those new personnel, that new shift?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came together again with Zeljko Meakic, because on that first day, he would come and go on several occasions to the investigation centre, to and from the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that while he was absent he was organising things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that specifically. I can just assume that he probably contacted some people in positions of responsibility to find out what was happening, because it was my impression that many things were not clear to him either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That first day that you spent in the Omarska Investigation Centre, did investigators appear?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said you went home to rest overnight. When did you come back to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find Mr. Meakic there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a change of shift organised again; that is, the night-shift being over, so new reinforcements had to come in? Who was doing that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the new morning shift appeared, who were to work that whole day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was food organised for the detainees on that day? Because you told us that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, as far as I was able to see, Milan Andzic from Omarska, as a private individual who was a wealthy, well-known businessman, brought several sacks full of sandwiches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those sandwiches, were they distributed among the detainees on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the distribution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen providing security. And I know that there were remarks that the food was insufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the food for the policemen organised on that second day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the investigating centre itself there was no food provided for the policemen on that day either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether some policemen had brought some food with them from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was visible. Almost everyone had a parcel in his pocket, a sandwich or something to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the policemen were told that there would be no food provided and that they should bring some from home?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we have been talking about two days now. In the course of those two days, did any new detainees appear in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that first day, the 28th to the 29th, there were none. On the 30th, on the second day, the 30th of May, late in the afternoon, sometime around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., some people arrived, that is, detainees, in several buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen in Prijedor before these new detainees were brought in on several buses, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, at around midday, amongst us policemen, the news was spreading that there had been an attack on Prijedor. There were announcements to that effect on the radio, some people heard these announcements, and listening to the radio that we had in one of the premises, according to the conversations being conducted within the territory of Prijedor, one could infer that a conflict was ongoing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This radio station that you mentioned, we'll be coming back to that -- the radio transmitter is something we'll be coming back to. My question is: Was an announcement issued to members of the security, that is, members of the Omarska Police Department? Was this announcement made to them, or did you learn it by listening in to others and their conversations over the radio transmitter?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no announcements made to the investigating centre itself. We were just able to overhear what other people were saying in the territory of Prijedor, because the same frequencies were being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, on the 30th of May, 1992, did the members of the Omarska police station department receive any kind of news, through Meakic or anyone else, that new detainees were arriving?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I simply heard nothing about that, nor did anyone inform me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a surprise for the security personnel to see these new detainees arriving?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all asking ourselves, "What is this?" and "What's happening?" and "Why again?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these men, was Mr. Meakic there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening, on that day, he was present too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, let's go back for a moment because we omitted something. What were you doing during that day until the arrival of these new detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on duty, as I had been the previous day, with the same orders from Zeljko, to lend a helping hand to the reserve policemen, should they need advice in performing their duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, did you move around on the pista, or did you spend the day inside?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent most of the day outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting, but again we have counsel basically testifying for the witness, putting in facts that are not in evidence. We would ask that he not ask leading questions and perhaps confine himself to asking the witness what the witness did, instead of stating what he believes the witness did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard the objection, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my mistake. I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing, Mr. Kvocka, during that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, the 30th of May, I spent doing the same things as I had done the previous day. I was on duty in the investigation centre, having the same assignments that I had been given by Mr. Meakic. I spent the time mostly outside, on the compound. Among the reserve policemen, no one came to ask for my assistance or advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time the buses with the new detainees arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in front of the entrance to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who escorted this convoy of detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The escort consisted of the police officers from Prijedor -- this I know because I recognised some of them as career policemen -- and also there were some military police. In other words, it was a mixed escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the commanding police officers from the Prijedor police station among them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of the top commanders whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the detainees who were brought in by bus?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken by these police officers who escorted them to certain rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were only the escorting police officers involved in this, in other words, those who were not members of the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you. The question that you have just asked is clearly a leading question, if you say "Was it these policemen who were doing this or that?" You must ask "Who did such and such?" If you're asking, "Did these police officers do this?" the answer will be yes. So you must ask, "Who did such and such?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will rephrase the question again, accepting the suggestion with gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the police officers from the escort who took the newly arrived prisoners to the places where they were first accommodated, and then they were also assisted by the police officers who were already there as security, in other words, in that area where they were placed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those buses, did you recognise any individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, on the 30th, these early arrivals -- the first arrival of those buses, yes, there were people I recognised, people whom I occasionally would meet in town. And those who were the most familiar to me, if I may go on, who had been brought in at that time, were my wife's three brothers: Adnan Crnalic, called Dado; Rizak Crnalic, also known as Rica; and Nedzad Crnalic, also known as Necko. Before I observed them, a police officer, who was an active duty police officer from Prijedor, whom I knew from before, Obrenko Sajdel, pointed them out to me, he said that they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised by this fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was absolutely surprised, and I started asking myself why were they brought in, why were any of these people brought to me, but especially them. I was upset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction in this situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply separated them out off -- I separated them out off to the side, and about ten minutes later I put them in an official vehicle and I took them out of there. I took them to my family house in Omarska, in other words, to my parents' house in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask anyone for permission to do so?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time. Zeljko was somewhere in the vicinity, but I did not go over to him to ask him anything. I did it spontaneously, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a violation of rules?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that this was some kind of a violation of rules, because I was taking a step which I was not entitled to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took your brothers-in-law home, did you come back to the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. After I dropped them off there -- and let me say right away that my wife and my children were already there in my parents' house, and we had a scene there between them because my wife had also heard on the radio that the general war had started and that bad things were happening in Prijedor, and she became quite frightened for her family and for her own safety in Prijedor on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife know where her brothers were during these operations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: She knew nothing until I brought them to my parents' home, and that is where she saw them for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you went back to Omarska, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my return, I stayed there very briefly because Zeljko told me that I was free and that I should report back the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him about your action with regard to your brothers-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not specifically, nor did I tell him anything about it, but I concluded that he must have received information about it while I was gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to stay in this area for a while. You're talking about the Omarska police station security. In these two days that you have just spent there, was there any additional security there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those two days, I noticed no other security except for the police officers from the Omarska precinct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a security guard. The company guard, was at the front gate.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a single company guard who was not part of the police security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was this front gate from the administration building? You said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 1.5, 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In addition to this company guard, was there another guard who was added at the front gate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no other guards except for that single guard at the front gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the 31st now. Can you describe how the guard shifts were organised? Without repeating what you said before.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st I reported to work again. I was met by Zeljko. He told me the same thing, that is, repeated the same orders. He said that I was duty officer and that he was just going to take a little rest, and during the day he had a lot of obligations, that the number of detainees had increased, that he had to do something with respect to increasing security and perhaps make certain changes in the method of work, and he left, but he told me he would just take a quick rest and that he would come back very shortly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the food supply organised? This is now the third day. Were detainees getting any food?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that third day, the food for detainees had already been provided. It was distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who organised the food, that is, the provisions for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much about this organisation. I know only that as early as 10.00 or 11.00 that morning, the containers with prepared food had arrived to this restaurant which we had shown yesterday, and the food distribution to the detainees had begun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice who had delivered the food, members of what structure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was brought in by a company vehicle, I think a vehicle belonging to that same company. I think it was a yellow -- painted yellow. I think that all mining company vehicles were painted yellow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the vehicle was owned by the company?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who drove this vehicle and to what organisation or structure did he belong?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but he was not a member of the police force. He was not a policeman. He wore a blue worker's suit; he did not wear any uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the company provide for food? Did they organise food distribution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously, during the regular operation of the company, they had organised cafeteria and food distribution for the entire company. This food preparation station was right by the front gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right by the front gate, about 1.5 to 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice what that first meal was? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I paid no attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the security receive any food that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Food was made available to them if they wanted to, and I think some of them did take it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was on the 31st. Were new detainees brought in? Did new buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the afternoon, somewhere around 1700, between 1700 and 1800, a couple of buses arrived with men who were then detained in this complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three or four buses, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they filled with people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was escorting those buses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those buses were escorted by police officers from Prijedor mixed in with military personnel. Some were described as military police and some described them as civilians, but those terms were used interchangeably in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the police officials, that is, Prijedor police officials who may have been escorting this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not recognise any of the police officials from Prijedor that I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone abuse or mistreat detainees as they were getting off the buses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were getting off the buses, I did not notice any mistreatment, but then at one point a very ugly and bad incident happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What incident?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will describe this incident. People started getting off one of the buses. I believe that in front of it was an empty bus which had already been emptied of people, and behind the bus from which people were disembarking there was another bus where people were still waiting to get off. As they were stepping off that middle bus, at one point a vehicle appeared from the direction where one entered the entire compound and a vehicle approached these buses. The driver came out of this vehicle, which was some kind of a pick-up truck, with a rifle in his hand and raged. He said, "Serbs, move away," and he started shooting at the people who were getting off the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in order not to go back through the details, maybe we can just stop here. We need a description of this rifle. I know this is a very ugly scene but try to just concentrate on this now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a rifle known as PAM, very similar to a regular automatic rifle but with a somewhat longer barrel. At the top of the barrel there is a bipod, something that can be used as support, as far as I understand its use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man who jumped out of this vehicle, who was enraged, can you tell us anything else about him that is out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when I started towards him, I could notice that he was quite inebriated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you go on now from the moment when he started shooting? Did he shoot at the people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I noticed him coming out and raising his weapon, I started towards him from his side, but he had already begun shooting. I approached him from his side, and the casings were already falling in my direction, and one brushed my face and scratched my face. I jumped in front of him about two metres. He still had his barrel trained in front. I opened my jacket, and I opened it and I told him, "What's with you, man? These are civilians. If you need to, shoot at me." For several seconds he stared at me. I did not know what he was going to do. However, he slowly put down the weapon and started crying, and he said, "They killed my brother." As he started putting down the weapon, I seized the weapon and I yanked it out of his arms. Zeljko Meakic then approached, and I handed him the rifle. A police investigator then approached, and later I was told that he had watched this incident from a window. Zeljko then turned over the rifle to him, and with the assistance of several other policemen, he took away this man and he basically arrested him, as I would call it in police parlance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you were both upset and frightened. Did you see the consequences of this shooting? Did you see how many people were hit and were they seriously injured?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he shot at people before I stepped in front of him, five or six people were injured. They all fell to the ground. As soon as Zeljko took this person away, together with some other reserve officers, I went to see if we could help these people, and it was clear that there were some very badly wounded ones among these five or six people. There were some who were sitting on the ground and holding onto the wounds, but there were a couple of them who were on the ground without any signs of life. As the reservists stayed with the less seriously wounded, I went to the room on the top floor where we had a radio transmitter, where we could call in to the Omarska police precinct, and I called the duty officer and I told him to immediately go to the health centre, which is about 50 metres from the police precinct. There was no other link to the health centre anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Can you tell the Chamber who was the duty officer in the precinct of whom you requested to provide an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Boro Delic, called Baja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did an ambulance arrive? When did it arrive, and who was the driver of this ambulance or what type of vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After awhile, about 15 minutes, an ambulance arrived but not a regular civilian ambulance vehicle. It was a much larger vehicle, a military ambulance vehicle, drab olive in colour, which had a lot of space for the wounded, and it was driven by a man from Omarska, a young man called Rosic. That's his last name. But we all knew him by his nickname which was Mingo. Those individuals were immediately carried into the vehicle, and Mingo drove them off in the direction of the front gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was injured during this bad incident?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The active duty policeman Branislav Bojic was also grazed by a bullet casing, like I was, and Miroslav Nisic, another police officer, was hit in the heel. The injury was such that he could not support himself on that leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he also provided assistance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he was taken in another vehicle, not in the same vehicle as those injured detainees were. He had an official vehicle made available to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Bojic was there. Who else was present during this serious incident?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among those present was a man called Rosic, who was not a member of the Omarska police precinct, but he was a company employee. He was a maintenance person, I think, at some water pump stations or something, he was employed there. He was in the vicinity, I noticed him and his son, who was also not a member of the police force but who apparently had just come to visit him and bring him some food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zeljko Meakic present at the time of this incident, or did he appear later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I took away the rifle from the person who was shooting, I saw Zeljko right next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the medical attention or therapy of Miroslav Nisic take?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Miroslav Nisic never rejoined the police force following this injury because it was a very complicated injury which he sustained to his heel, and long after this, I saw him hobble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the other members of the reserve police force towards that incident?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the people that I talked to directly were astounded, one and all. Others, some of them would say, "Go to Gradacac and fight there. Don't shoot at civilians," that kind of thing. They were angry, they were bitter. They asked themselves, "If things carry on this way, how are we going to be able to work at all, how are we going to do our job," things like that. The comments were along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to that individual after the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what happened in those couple of minutes. He went off together with the inspector and Zeljko, he went off with them, and after that, he was taken away from the compound by the policemen. What happened later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you yourself feel, faced with a situation of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to describe my feelings after so many years, ten years, but traces, of course, remain. It was a great shock for me. It was the first time in my entire police career that I was faced with a situation of this kind and conduct of this kind, with a killing before my very eyes. Briefly speaking, I was confused. There was total confusion in my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I see that Mr. Kvocka is a little tired. It is his third day of testimony. Perhaps we have to bear that in mind. But in any event, before the break, I should like to share with you a few thoughts. We are truly at the beginning of this trial, we are going to have many days of work, and I think it is always important to establish or to forecast a few things which can be contained within certain rules. In order to establish certain rules of communication amongst us, I should like to go back to this question of leading or non-leading questions. I think you, as the attorneys, are professionals -- I mean attorneys on both sides -- highly experienced, highly competent lawyers, and you know very well, from the point of view of verbal communication, what is a leading question and a non-leading question. I think that the goodwill of Ms. Hollis and Mr. Keegan have allowed certain other leading questions to pass. On the whole, I must tell you, Mr. Simic, that you have done a very good job of your examination-in-chief, but I should like to make two points to refine the criteria. Instead of asking "Were you surprised?" what you should ask is "What was your reaction?" Because in the totality of a whole range of reactions, there can be a wide variety of reactions, joy, surprise, et cetera. If you choose one and focus on surprise, then the answer can be either yes or no. If it is yes, one will never know whether there were any other reactions; if no, again, we will not know. So I think that is one example. Another example that I would like to use is the following: Does this represent a violation of the rules? For instance, the question should have been, how do rules provide for such a situation? Otherwise, if there are several possibilities, you are obviously choosing one. There is really no need for me to explain these things to you because you are highly competent, highly experienced, you know these things very well, but in the course of a conversation, one may have an immediate reaction which does not necessarily fit within this framework and can be considered a leading question, and we understand that. But a second point that I should like to consider with you is the following: In principle, a person, a witness who's testifying for several days, I think it is really too much to ask for him to testify for more than an hour at a time. It's different when we have a witness coming for one day only. So I would like to give you the following suggestion: Psychologists, the people working on these things, say that after an hour and ten minutes of work, the concentration, the efficiency, declines. So there is no point in insisting on working for longer than one hour and ten minutes at a time. As a general orientation, I would suggest the following: We'll work for one hour ten, one hour twenty minutes, and it is up to you, as soon as we reach one hour ten minutes -- we're talking about the normal situation, when witnesses come here for one day or so -- between one hour ten and one hour twenty as a working period, you choose the moment where we should break, because I think it is also important to bear in mind that there are segments of information that one wants to cover in a certain period. So you choose the moment in between one hour ten, one hour twenty to make the interruption, or I shall show you this sign [indicates], the time-out sign, by hand, indicating that we could take a break. But it is up to you to decide. So I think from the point of view on ensuring an orderly, quiet proceedings, we should bear all these things in mind. There's one other thing I wanted to say. I prefer to have more shorter breaks, but I know that from the point of the accused it is complicated to have such short breaks, and therefore respecting the right of the accused to a break as well, we need at least a 20-minute break for them to be able to leave the courtroom, to take a rest, to be able to follow their trial. So as we go along and come up with questions of this kind, we can regulate them so as to have a certain code of communication, so we will know in advance what is going to happen and what the solution is. Let us now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Kvocka, you may sit down too. Mr. Simic, it's your turn. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for the suggestions you have made. Despite all our experience, this is one new experience for us, and we always learn something new and are faced with new situations. So thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what happened afterwards? How did you organise the rest of your day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, when I left my three brothers-in-law in the house and after the short conversations that we had and the meetings with their sister, that is to say, my wife, and that little -- and the confusion over that whole situation, they were happy to see each other again, and sorry and sad because they didn't know what happened to the others. I returned to the investigation centre. I found Zeljko there again. It was 7.00 or half past 7.00 in the evening by that time. He told me, because I was working that entire day, that I should go off duty, on leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This brings us to the 1st of June. Could you describe your activities in the course of that day, the 1st of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned and slept through the night, spent the night in my parents' place in Omarska, together with all the other people there. On the 1st, I went back to my job in the morning once again. However, in the evening, the previous evening, we were, of course, all there in the house, and I was in a difficult psychological situation. I remember that I didn't really have much inclination to talk to anybody else, so that my wife tried her best to make me enter into the conversation. She would ask me whether I would like a cup of coffee or things like that, but I just wanted to be left alone. I laid down on the floor in the room, turned towards the floor, and I tried to collect my thoughts and to see what I was going to do in the future if faced with that kind of situation because, quite obviously, there were going to be a lot of problems for my family, my wife's family. I succeeded in having a bit of a rest in the course of the night, and in the morning, on the 1st, I returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your job?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that when I arrived on duty, I felt even worse than I had the previous night. Zeljko saw that there was something wrong with me. We had a short conversation, and I had the feeling that he understood me. He told me that I should take two or three days off, not to come to work for two or three days. So I went back to Omarska, to the house in which my brothers-in-law were accommodated and my parents, and we discussed the situation. They were all crying. They wondered what had happened to their wives, to their mother who had stayed on in Prijedor, what had happened to one of their children. One of the brothers-in-law had a child at the time. They wondered what had happened to them. That's what we did, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife and I decided to go to Prijedor at this point and to go directly to the house of my mother-in-law, but we didn't find anybody at home. So we went to my flat, which is at Pecani, and that's where we found them; that is to say, there were two daughters-in-law, that is, the wives of my wife's brothers. We found their wives, two of the wives there. We also came across my mother-in-law, my wife's mother. Her name is Hajra. And there were some more elderly woman there as well. I knew some of them, others I did not. At the same time, like us, they were happy to see us. But at the same time, they were a little frightened, and they had many questions that they wanted to ask us, and wondered what had happened to their sons or husbands. So they were worried about their whereabouts. We managed to calm them down and to tell them that they were safe, at least for the time being, that we felt they were safe, and that we would see what would happened. So I used those two or three days that I was given leave to go back to Omarska. I took some food from my parents. They had a large garden in Omarska, because it's a village, a rural area. It's not purely a town. So you could grow things, and you didn't have to buy everything in the shops. So we took these things from the vegetable garden to Prijedor. There I came across my mother-in-law in her own home during the day, but once again there were quite a lot of neighbours there, mostly womenfolk, elderly women, her friends, and I knew perhaps two or three of them, but there were at least eight or ten of them there at the time. They told me that they had come to my mother-in-law's because they felt more or less safe while they were in her house. The wives of my brothers-in-law were still in my own flat, so we took them some food as well. So that's how those two or three days went by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you say that there were eight to ten elderly women neighbours and that they felt safer in your mother-in-law's house. Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my mother-in-law would say to me that when they come to her, they always ask whether they can come in and that they think they would be safe there. And they say, "Well, your son-in-law is a Serb, so they probably won't wish to harm us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were your sisters-in-law not in their own houses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did live in the same house earlier on, that is to say, where my mother-in-law lived, in that same house. But there wasn't enough room for everybody, and they too felt safer in my flat. However, we really didn't know how safe it was. That was a debatable point, because when these people turned up in my flat, I met some people standing guard in front of the entrance. They were reservists, reserve policemen. I knew them just in passing. They were just acquaintances. And they would say to me, "What are you doing?" I apologise for the expressions that I'm going to use; I apologise to the Trial Chamber. They said, "What are you doing, you fag? You're keeping flats in your -- you're keeping Turks in your flat," and they would use similar derogatory terms. "You bastard," they would say to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I know that it is difficult for all of us to talk about those truly terrible times which we all hope will never recur, but I think that this is a good point to broach a very important question: Who organised the camp, how everything functioned. To do this, I would like to resort to some documents which I consider to be very significant and which will help us to understand the whole workings and system of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is DP55. The document is DP55, and I would like to ask the usher to distribute the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence Exhibit D17/1, and D17/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have in front of you a letter of the public security station of Prijedor, dated the 31st of May 1992. When and where did you see this letter for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this letter for the first time when the gentleman from the Prosecutor's Office showed me it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have probably read the letter, so I'm not going to ask you that. Who was the founder of the collection and investigating centre in the Omarska compound, according to this letter?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this letter, I am able to conclude -- but I'd rather say that this is an order, because it states that something is being ordered. A letter is something different. The founder of the investigating centre or camp or whatever you like to call it was the crisis staff or the chief of the public security station, Simo Drljaca, whose signature is at the end of this letter and who is the person who issued this order. But in view of the fact that he refers to a decision taken by the crisis staff in this particular order, then I cannot differentiate as to who was the founder and who was the commander of the camp. Judging by the general situation that prevailed at the time and in my talks with people, I should also like to say that that could have been Simo Drljaca, in view of the fact that everybody used to say that without his permission, nothing could be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, does this order contain any orders issued to the police precinct of the police station of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Drljaca, in fact, order the police station of Omarska to do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca -- I think it is in paragraph 6 -- is issuing strict orders to the security services at the collection centre, and I see another term used for the camp. Here it states "collection centre": "Shall be provided by the Omarska police station."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what does it mean to provide security for the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, briefly speaking, it means that the policemen belonging to this police station and its precinct are duty-bound to provide security, that is to say, prevent individuals from escaping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this order contained in paragraph 6 imply that it is -- does it imply any organisational activities for the policemen of that department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No that does not emanate from this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was dated the 31st of May 1992. On the last page, it stipulates to whom the copies were sent; that is to say, which individuals received copies of this order from Mr. Drljaca. Who received this order of Mr. Drljaca, dated the 31st of May 1992 for the security services. Can you recognise the signature of the individuals who received these orders on behalf of the security service?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 1, it states that Zeljko Meakic took over the order, and it is his signature for the security service. I also know the signature under number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the signature of Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Meakic on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the police department in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In keeping with the rules and regulations of the service, bearing in mind the orders contained in paragraph 6, that this order should be received by the commander of the police station of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the responsible individual for organising security, the security provided for by the police station of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is responsible for the policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we broached the subject of security, security by the policemen of the security station of Omarska. Was that the sole form of security that existed at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my return from, let us say my leave, which wasn't really a resting period for me, it was the three or four days that I found very difficult, but noticed, on the first day after I had come back to work, I noticed certain changes that had taken place in the work of the police at the investigating centre. And there were other changes as well with respect to the security system for the investigation centre. Would you like me to tell you what these changes were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the changes that had taken place in the overall security system at the centre, and what innovations were made?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as I went through the entrance gate, I noticed that in addition to the company guard, from the mine, that is, there was also a policeman standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, the Omarska Police Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I moved towards the investigation centre, when I was halfway there, that is to say, midway between the entrance gate and the building, there was a facility of some kind, a sort of petrol pump or something like that, that's what it was referred to, and there were three or four soldiers standing there of the Territorial Defence. Because at the time we used the terms -- either we referred to it as the army or the Territorial Defence, both these two terms were used interchangeably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, at this second guard checkpoint, during your stay in Omarska, was there a member of the department of the Omarska police station at any time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other changes with respect to the overall compound that you noted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious that on the broader area, especially on this side here [indicates], where that green surface is on the model, but quite far off, that there were also groups of two or three men belonging to the army, military personnel. And afterwards, people would say that groups of people were all around the compound, although we couldn't see that standing in front of the compound itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you actually see among those security officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw those that I had to pass by, and I saw these others at the edge of the meadow, and also at one other place. There is another access road here [indicates], in this direction, one might say at right angles in relation to the road leading from the main entrance, and there were military there too, but some distance away from the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other new security guards within the compound?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the compound, among the guards, the policemen, I noticed quite a number of new faces. But they were not properly dressed as policemen, they were mostly wearing military uniforms, green uniforms, the uniforms worn by the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were those men? Did they belong to your police department or were they new?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko said that they were people who had been attached from the Territorial Defence to assist in providing security, and some of them had been newly mobilised reserve policemen. However, there was another group of policemen in addition to these who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of policemen wearing blue police uniforms but in camouflage colours of blue. So they weren't plain blue, but coloured in different shades, but blue. And we were told that these were members of a special unit from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were in this unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to estimate the number, but there were at least 30 of them. They also had their two combat vehicles there. There were the complete crews of these vehicles, and these vehicles are manned by four to five men each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those combat vehicles, in the former system that you're familiar with, did they belong to the standard police armaments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police in those days did not have combat vehicles as part of its standard equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe those two combat vehicles and the weapons they were armed with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them is known, I think, as a personnel carrier. It is used for the transportation of men on the inside, and it has caterpillar wheels, not normal rubber tyres, one of these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it an armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's armour on the roof with a weapon mounted, a certain type of weapon of which I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a large-calibre weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also large in size, larger than a normal rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be a machine-gun, a small cannon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like a machine-gun. Something like a machine-gun, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second vehicle, could you describe that one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second vehicle is what is known as BOV, I think that is the expression used. It is also a vehicle equipped on the roof with a heavy-calibre weapon, but it has rubber tyres, not caterpillar wheels like the previous one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the leader or commander of this special police unit that you came across among the security force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those first seven days that this group was there for, the leader was a certain man called Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, that group was replaced later on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were replaced about six or seven days later, and another group appeared, again from Banja Luka, wearing the same kind of uniforms and with the same vehicles. Their leader was somebody called Strazivuk, that was his surname, Strazivuk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about the system of security, could you comment on the relationship between Meakic and Maric or Strazivuk? Who was the superior to whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think neither of the two could give orders to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When entering the Omarska compound, what is the Omarska police controlling through its members? Which access points?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was controlling only the entrance gate. This policeman who was now positioned there, he could control entry into the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other entrances? Who controlled the possibility of entering the compound from other directions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were members of the special police from Banja Luka actually doing in practice? What were their assignments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have guard posts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for these two vehicles which were positioned in certain places and manned by their crews. The others moved around the investigation centre freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any problems because of their presence there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number of problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they roamed around the investigation centre freely, they would go from one building to another. There were reports that they mistreated people; that of their own initiative, they conducted certain investigations; that they confiscated money and jewellery; that during their so-called investigations, they would beat up people. There were certain situations when Zeljko didn't know what to do because there were clashes between the policemen from the Omarska department and them; first verbal exchanges, of course, because I didn't see any physical fights, nor did anyone dare to oppose them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the attitude taken by the other guards in relation to the conduct of the members of the special police from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other guards kept their distance. They said if things continued in that way, they would simply walk out, they would give up their jobs, they didn't know what to do, that things couldn't go on like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your contacts like with members of this police force, if any?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, I spoke to Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What prompted the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One morning, I was informed, or rather a prisoner complained to me as I passed by him, a prisoner whom I knew well, his name was Dedo Crnalic who is a relative of my wife's, though not a close one, he complained to me that during the night money had been taken from him and a ring and a watch. He said that the watch was more of a souvenir than something of value, at least that's what he told me. But he wanted to let me know that that wasn't all that important, so long as things didn't get worse. And he said that this had been done by the people wearing blue camouflage uniforms, because this is something he could clearly see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when I talked to Maric, who, in my assessment, was quite a decent man, and he told me literally that these were gangs out of control, that this unit was a gang of men out of control, and that he would see if he could restore to this person the things that had been taken away from him. I think that after some time, some of those things were restored to him, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if this will not be too complicated, I should like to tender a new exhibit, but I would like to keep the previous exhibit because we will be coming back to it. So the next document is the Defence document number 54.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence Exhibit 18/1; 18/1A for the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what was Mr. Meakic's attitude towards the members of this special unit from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he too was dissatisfied with their conduct. He was confused, upset, disturbed. He said that he had to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he contact Mr. Drljaca for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the members of this special unit from Banja Luka leave Omarska for good?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left -- or this second shift of them, they left when their shift ended, and that was perhaps one day less than seven days, a day or two less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough idea when that could have been?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th or the 13th. Perhaps the 14th. I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the month of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have before you a letter addressed by Mr. Drljaca to the head of the Security Services Centre, Banja Luka. Could you read that letter through, though you have had occasion to read it before. It was produced by the Prosecution. What is stated in this letter, is it true? Were there problems as Mr. Drljaca described them to the head of this unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read this letter, and it roughly corresponds to what I have just said. He said that this was a unit whose members were commanded by Strazivuk. So this is the second shift I was describing, that they were interrogating people, mistreating them, that they were simply seizing money and other valuables. This unit did even worse things under the control of Strazivuk than the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that completes the part of the testimony relating to the presence of the special police unit in Omarska. So could the usher put back the previous document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, which document are we dealing with now? What is the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our number 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the last one, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is Exhibit D17/1, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph 7, please. To whom does this order assign the duty of organising meals in the Omarska compound?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is that the mine's management, and allow me to read it: "Shall organise meals for investigators, guards, and detainees, according to norms which shall be agreed with the military quartermaster service. At the same time, the mine's management shall organise regular cleaning, as well as maintenance of plumbing, electrical fixtures, and other utilities, and it shall organise other kinds of logistic support for the work and stay of the given number of persons on the given premises by obligatory work on the specialised employees."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the mine's management carry out its duties in accordance with these instructions in paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that they engaged in these activities, but to what extent they were successful is something I cannot judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Omarska compound fenced in with wire?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later was there any kind of fence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my sojourn there, there was never any kind of wire fence around it, around the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the compound mined to prevent escape? Do you have information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not mined. Nobody said anything to that effect. I could see people moving freely, military men walking around the area where we could see them. They moved there freely along that grass surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This order, does it give certain persons any specific tasks? You told us Zeljko Meakic was assigned the task of providing security. Are there any assignments to named individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone is given certain assignments contained in 16 or 17 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the superiors.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic was given these orders as you have described them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any coordinators?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, there is an instruction which says: "Continued work and selection of arrested persons shall be conducted by a mixed group of investigators of national, public, and military security who have to be organised along this same mixed principle, and the persons responsible for their work are Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about paragraph 17? Who supervises the implementation of this order?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that the implementation of this order should be supervised by police chief Dusan Jankovic, in collaboration with the Banja Luka Security Services Centre -- and the abbreviation is used, CSB -- with the support of authorised executive personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the responsible executive personnel from this decision with whom Mr. Dusan Jankovic should have organised this activity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring only to the policing segment, then Zeljko Meakic was his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the whole system, the system as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at it from a broader standpoint, then he should have coordinated with the manager of the mines, with the military command, and with possibly these executives or senior officials, whatever the term is used here, the coordinators of the service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the coordinators?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this decision issued to those persons who have certain assignments as superiors, with superior responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From signatures of the people who received these orders and from what is stated about to whom the decision was forwarded, we can see that those were the crisis staff; the coordinators; the CSB of Banja Luka; the police chief, that is Mr. Jankovic; the security chief, that is Zeljko Meakic; the general manager of the iron ore mines Ljubija and for the files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kvocka. But this document raises another issue that we have to deal with. Mention is made here of investigations. Where were investigations carried out, if any, in the Omarska compound?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the detainees were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which services conducted investigations of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the state security service. For a short period of time they were called national security service, and this is why I was mentioning that too, but that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many services are there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three separate services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of each of these services?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
