utterances.text: These coordinators, these three coordinators were the chiefs. Ranko Mijic was the head of the public security service, Mirko Jesic was the state security services chief, and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic was the head of the military services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these investigations organised? Who were the investigators? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have mentioned yesterday, the investigations took place in that upper floor of the administration building where there were a number of offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall how many offices there were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can remove the roof from the model so that the witness can better see and provide the information that we need. The administration building. The one next to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the layout of this floor correspond to the layout of the offices on the top floor of the administration building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it does correspond to what I was able to observe there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who used the upper-floor premises? What was used by the Omarska police and what was used by the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Omarska police used one room which is where the police officers were staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please show us that room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is supposed to be this room, B5 [indicates]. It is marked as B5 here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who used the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other rooms were used by the mixed investigation group. They used all of the other rooms. This is where they carried out investigations. There was a larger room at the end where the coordinators were sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the marking of that larger room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: B1. Actually, B1 was also used to mark -- but there was a sliding door which was separating these two areas of that room B1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the investigators come from to work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were bused in from Prijedor for a part of them. I don't know about every one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they come every morning?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except Sundays, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time would they come?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time did they stay?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Till 5.00 in the afternoon, 1700.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the investigation room we can skip, but how many investigators worked per room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three; it depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the composition of the investigation teams in each of the rooms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mixed. For instance, it would happen that an investigator from the public security service would work together with the state security service, and sometimes a third, a military one, would be added.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have note-takers or typists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two women who worked with typewriters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come on the same bus with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had worked -- in fact, one had worked in the public security station in Prijedor and the other one worked at the state security service. I knew this because they were there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavica Lakic and Nada Markovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they sit while they were in the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had -- in fact, they had two tables in the same office which occasionally were used by the police officers from the Omarska precinct. Yes, I remember. There were two desks arranged in an L-shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their task on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During their working hours, they were typing up documents, and I noticed that there were -- that handwritten drafts were brought to them by these coordinators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who among the Omarska police officers were staying in this room and what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officers were staying there, the duty police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that fall within the regular police duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any communication -- was there any communication equipment there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a radio transmitter, a so-called fixed-radio transmitter, and a local telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean, a "local telephone"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means you could make internal calls in the compound from that telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have made a call out to the Prijedor police station or the Omarska precinct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you communicate with those two offices?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the radio transmitter. That was a possibility, at least to call the Omarska precinct and the duty room in the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you called in for assistance, when that incident took place, who did you call? How did you make the call?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used that transmitter that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a code used to make calls?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the entire communications system, there are certain call codes. The term "code" was not used, it was just called a call number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the call number for the Omarska complex, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that right now. I believe that -- I think that the word "Sana" was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any numbers added to that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sana 5. I don't know whether this was Sana 5, but there was another number or digit in addition to the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would one need numbers in addition to the word "Sana," as you called it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there are a number of participants at the same frequency, and so that one would know which exact location it was. So, for instance, if you said Sana 5, that would be the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Sana 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sana 1 would then be the duty room in the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk about communications, to stay with that, was there any other telephone lines so that someone could make telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a telephone in the coordinator's office by which you could call outside of the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, from your duty room, call the front gate which we mentioned, that was 1.5 kilometres away from the administration building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was within the compound. So it was within the local system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have another few minutes before we take a break. I would like to ask you more about this room. Who were the duty police officers who were in this room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to myself, the duty also provided was Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, and Momcilo Gruban, also known as Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this communication system functioning by order? How did it function, this whole communication system, that is, of the compound with the outside world, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms, throughout my stay there, in my use of that room, it happened several times that someone would call from the Prijedor Public Security Station asking for Zeljko Meakic, and I only used it once when I asked for the ambulance when that incident occurred, when the injuries occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any reports drafted about the work of the security, and were you involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no documents kept or produced there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the security service have a list of detainees? Because these were detained persons there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that actually no list existed of detainees ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hierarchy of individuals whom we mentioned, Dusan Jankovic, then Mijic, Jesic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic, what was the status of Meakic, who was the commander of the Omarska police precinct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was subordinate to Jankovic, and as for his relationship with the coordinators, I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he have ordered anything to Mijic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have reached the 1.10-hours mark, and we may have become a little exhausted. We can move on to the methods of investigation after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. We are now going to have a 20-minute break, and then we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, you may continue, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, before the break, we had opened the question of the investigation. We will talk about the method of investigation and whether you have any knowledge of it. So this is how I'm going to begin. In what way were the detainees identified by the investigators, or whoever it was who identified them, how were they brought in? And can you give us an overview of the method of work of the investigation teams at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to describe it as best I can, what I knew at the time, based on what I was able to observe. Zeljko Meakic designated a group of police officers, eight to ten of them, and put them at the investigators' disposal. Then the investigators asked these police officers directly to bring in a certain individual for an interview. I observed that there were cases when they did not ask for someone by their name, but rather just said that people should be brought in in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the coordinators have a list of detainees in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After a request to bring in a specific or any detainee, what procedure was followed then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they conducted an information interview with the individual that was brought in to them, and the police officer would remain standing in front of the office, and sometimes even inside the office, together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a usual procedure? Was there any deviation from the regular police procedure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to determine this. I observed that they were brought in, escorted by police officers, and that then interviews were conducted with these individuals in the offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except for those ten or so police officers that you mentioned, did other police officers have access to the area where the investigations took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those who were on their guard positions did not have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the duty officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This may be obvious, but let me ask you this anyway: Were the security officers at Omarska involved in any way in the investigations against these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. There were even suggestions on the part of Zeljko Meakic that any contact with detainees should be avoided, unless the detainees approached them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that Zeljko's order, or did it come from some superior place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko passed it on to us, but I don't know if it went up -- if it came from above or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any mistreatment of detainees during the investigations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay up there, I observed a situation which, to me, looked like something like that. What happened was I was sitting in the duty room, and some unusual noises could be heard, I could describe them as moans, from the area of the offices on the same side where the police duty room was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you react to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stepped out into the hallway to see what was going on and I entered several offices. In several of the offices, everything was fine, but in one of the offices, I could see that one of the persons being interrogated had been beaten up. And then I reacted, and I think that it was rather harsh, my reaction, I said, "What is going on?" and I asked whether a police officer or a reserve police officer was involved in this in any way. There was an investigator there whom I did not know -- he was not from Prijedor because I know all those from Prijedor -- and he kind of laughed a little bit at me, and he said, "It's fine. It's fine. Everything is going to be all right." But I didn't get -- I couldn't get a good impression of who it was that had beaten up the detainee, whether it was the police officer who had brought him there or the investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you were in Omarska over a period of time. Did you hear any other noises, any other voices coming from the office, different offices? You would spend up to 10 hours there at a time. Were there any moans or cries or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This incident that I just described, that was very specific and I reacted on that occasion. But on several other occasions, I could surmise that force had been used also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the police force of the former Yugoslavia, before these events, do you know of the use of force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you responded, when you felt provoked by the noises and moans, what was the response of other police officers, your colleagues? What did they do? Did they agree with your response, or did they just gloss it over? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number -- let me tell you. This created a lot of noise. I reacted rather harshly, so a number of doors opened and people stepped out to see. Those from Banja Luka, one of them said, "Listen, kid, what are you doing here? What are you trying to do?" And one of the investigators who worked -- who had a desk at the top of the hallway, this is where he conducted his investigations, and he is a local man from Prijedor, he supported me. He said, "Good for you, Kvocka."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the name of that police officer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the investigator?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Rade Knezevic. He worked in the Prijedor police force for a period of time. Later on, the two investigators who worked across from the police room, the officer's room, said it was all right for me to have responded, but what were they to do, because these investigators were not going to listen to us about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the subject of the investigation was? What were they trying to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know, except that people talked about the need to investigate these individuals to find out who took part in the attack and in the armed rebellion, who had organised it all, who had financed it, and things like that. This is what the word was about among the police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who received the investigators' reports?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were told in the beginning that this was going to take about 15 days, did you see any detainees released in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After about six or seven days of these, a larger group was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was released?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I believe they were taken in at least two buses. And the other detainees said that these people were, for the most part, from a place near Prijedor called Gornja Puharska. I believe that they were the first ones to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also individual releases?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, except that I observed that on two or three occasions the investigators would take someone in the bus which they used for their transportation. But it would also happen that in the morning they would also bring in a person or two on that same bus, when they were coming to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you pinpoint the time when any kind of release stopped?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say so. I think that there were no mass releases during my stay, except for that group which I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brothers-in-law were subject to an investigation. Were there any reactions on the part of Mr. Meakic with regard to their absence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Meakic told me, on several occasions, that, quite simply, the climate was such in Omarska -- it was not a good climate, that is to say, for me and my family. More for my family who was in a house in the centre of town, that there were rumours going around of various kinds that I was hiding -- that I was putting up extremists, that I was feeding them while their compatriots were being killed in other places. So criticisms of this kind were conveyed to me. Other people told me that too from town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regards to your brothers-in-law, were there any demands made, any conditions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, he told me that I must see what I was going to do because it wouldn't end up well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the release of the detainees, and we'll take up the subject of your brothers-in-law later on. Once again, I'd like to look at it from the aspect of the superiors in the Omarska compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this in view, I would like to tender DP21. It is our DP21. I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D19/1, Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have in front of you a decision of the crisis staff, dated the 2nd of June 1992, that is to say, from the very outset of the existence of this unfortunate centre. In Article 6 -- and I'd like to ask you to read it, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in Article 6: "This decision that the public security station is entrusted for the implementation of this decision and personal responsibilities held by the chief of the public security station which exclusively with his signature can release any individuals detained."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There seems to be a mix-up with the documents on the monitor. Just one moment, please, if we may, to clarify this. We apologise, Your Honours, because there were two similar documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I shall interpret this article. Who was the supreme authority, not to say the -- in charge of all the managerial structures in the Omarska compound?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says here, what the crisis staff wrote, we can see it is evident that it is the chief of the public security station himself who was responsible, and that he exclusively, by virtue of his signature, could make the moves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. We may be able to assist you in the mix-up in the documents. I believe we have an English translation of the proper document if you wish to have that placed on the ELMO. I don't know if that would assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it too, but it will be a good idea. Any assistance is welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have the document now, Ms. Hollis. We have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We were the only ones confused by it, Your Honour. I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you anyway, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, who is the individual who was solely responsible for the release from Omarska of any individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief of the public security station himself, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask, and I hope that we're not going to have any more technical problems, to take a look at document 25. It is our number 25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence Exhibit D20/1, D20/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have before you a letter, a report to the crisis staff of the municipal assembly of Prijedor, dated the 1st July 1992, submitted by Mr. Simo Drljaca. I should like to ask you to read the first paragraph or item in this letter which has to do with what we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that: "Conclusion number 01-111-108/92, by which the release of prisoners is prohibited, is being fully observed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the security service, any policemen, or Meakic as the head of the department, commander of the department, have any knowledge of the existence of an absolute prohibition for the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This sentence, what does it assert, confirm? Who remains the supreme authority when it comes to the release of individuals from Omarska? Who is master of life and death in Omarska, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this just confirms that it was Simo Drljaca. Simo Drljaca was the sole individual who could order or sign any kind of document ordering the release of somebody from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the context of these questions, I should like to refer to document DP24.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence Exhibit D21/1 and D21/1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you now have before you an order of the crisis staff of the Prijedor municipality, dated the 2nd of July, 1992. This is also a document which we received in the disclosure process from the Prosecution. You said a moment ago that security, that is to say, the police precinct, did not have a list or information as to who the detainees were. Does paragraph 2, point 2, of this order contain an answer to the question who had the lists and records of the individuals who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had the lists, the lists with the names of individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here that "Information about these workers is to be submitted by the public security station" of Prijedor "on request of the above-mentioned organs, companies, and associations."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the top right-hand corner, we have a list of the individuals to whom copies of this order were sent. Can you identify these people and tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The first two are fairly legible. They are Marko Dzenadija and number 2 is Dusan Jankovic. It says "D. Jankovic," but I think it means Dusan Jankovic. And under number 3, it could be M. Topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marko Dzenadija, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a worker from previous times. He worked in the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, when the secretariat existed, and the public security of Prijedor later on which came into being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 2, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3, "M. Topic," do you know that individual?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be a woman. She was a clerk, an administrator, in Drljaca's office, because there was a lady with the surname Topic, and she was a sort of technical secretary to Drljaca, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this order sent to Mr. Meakic, the head of security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to wind up this subject of investigation and interviews. The duty officers were in the same room as two typists; was that so throughout your stay at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what they were writing down or typing out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we had any insight into that, because once they had completed their work, typing out the document, they would send them back to the coordinators. Perhaps if anybody was interested, they could just have a brief look, glance at the paper in the typewriter, but as far as I was able to note, this wasn't of interest to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your brothers-in-law subject to an interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When rumours were going around Omarska about the problems that I and my family could face, I contacted two inspectors, investigators whom I knew and who previously worked in Prijedor. They are younger men, that is to say, they didn't have many years of service, and I knew them to be very proper in their conduct and in conducting the interviews. So I asked them whether they could interview my brothers-in-law and to tell me when to bring them in for questioning. They told me that I could bring them in straightaway, that there was no problem, so that that is what I did. Having completed the interviews with those inspectors, I took my brothers-in-law back to the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the inspectors tell you about the results of the interviews at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Nebojsa Tomicic, and the other one's name is Babic, he was also Nebojsa Babic, they told me that they had nothing interesting to note and that my brothers-in-law were absolutely of no interest to them from any aspect, but that they could do nothing else. All they could do was to send them back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned for the second time the unpleasantness that you could have, and that people told you that you would have some unpleasantness. Could you tell us, who told you this and when?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the unpleasantness and what Mr. Meakic told me, and some of my neighbours who indirectly let this be understood, that the situation was not a good one, that the mood was not good, on one occasion in Omarska, one of my school friends looked me up -- at the beginning of his career, he worked with me in Prijedor but then went to work in Banja Luka -- it was about the 12th or 13th of June, I believe. We met in the centre of Omarska, and as we hadn't seen each other for a long time, for about a year, we went to have a cup of coffee. He explained to me briefly that he had come to visit his wife, who was in a nearby village, near Omarska, the village's name is Piskavica, and the name of that friend of mine was Jadranko Mikic. So after a brief discussion about general subjects, he said to me -- well, he became a little more serious, and he said, "Well, pal," he used this word "pal," sort of classmate, "in Banja Luka, in our security centre, people are saying bad things about you, they're not saying nice things about you. You haven't got a good reputation. They're saying that you are a greater enemy to the Serbs than the Muslims are themselves, that you are collaborating with them, that you're helping them in every respect," something along those lines, that's what he said to me on the occasion. He also said that rumour had it in Banja Luka that, quite simply, I was collaborating with another school friend of ours, and he said that they knew in Banja Luka that this particular school friend of ours was a sniper in the Green Berets, and that I was a great collaborator of his. And he said, "That's all I can tell you. Even I've said too much already, it's dangerous for me. But as we're colleagues and friends, take care of yourself. The times are bad. And good luck to you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the term you used "klasic" mean, when you referred to your pal or classmate? Tell us what the term "klasic" means.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the term was used between people who had completed school in the same class or level, especially when it came to the police school and the cadets there, and for uniformed personnel, because that's how they referred to each other, they went to the same class. So it's a friendly term for people you were in the same class with, on a par with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a friendly term, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what effect did this have on you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of everything that had taken place previously, this was another blow, another additional shock, because up till then, I thought that this was a small circle of people who thought that way and that these -- well, shall I say, threats that were addressed to me, I didn't take them seriously up until that moment. I tried to clear things up for me in my own mind, what I was doing that was considered to be so terrible, and I couldn't really see what it was that I was doing wrong, the reasons for these criticisms to have been made of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I think this rounds off the subject of investigators and inspectors, but let us go back to a question we touched upon earlier on. What did you do to solve the problem of your brothers-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all this information that had reached me, and after talking to Zeljko, he told me, "Well, I can't tell you anything. You know what Simo's like yourself. If you want to go and ask him," and "Come what may." He also told me that Zeljko wouldn't dare go up to him with any question of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Simo Drljaca from before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until he came to be the chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a new man in the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a completely new man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have enough willpower to go and see him, guts to go and see him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the conversation like? How did it end?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One morning, I managed to reach Simo Drljaca, having asked the secretary to announce me, and I went into his office, he just said, "What's up, Kvocka?" and I tried to explain to him that I had a problem and that I would like to return my brothers-in-law to their own homes, that they were interviewed in Omarska by inspectors and that they said that they had done nothing wrong, and could he issue a permit to that effect. After my first introductory statements and my requests, he jumped out of his chair, and said, "What's wrong with you, Kvocka? The Muslims seem to have got your brain." He said, "Well, perhaps you're not a Serb actually at all. Take your pants off so I can see. Perhaps you're a Muslim yourself. I could deal with you very easily were it not for some other people here in SUP, in the police station." He said, "Get out and don't come back again. I don't want to see you again."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing. I was astounded by his behaviour, the reaction on the part of a leader. I had never encountered that in my entire career before. So I went back to Omarska. I went to work to do my shift, went on duty. I was with Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell anybody in your family about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I told my wife, in general terms, what had happened, because she asked me how we were going to solve the whole situation, that was terrible for these people in Omarska, they didn't dare leave the house, they were frightened to leave the house and go anywhere. When I told her that I had not been able to do anything and not been able to secure their official release, they were very surprised, astonished, because we just didn't see a way out of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your brothers-in-law? Did they learn of how things stood?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think my wife told them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next with respect to your brothers-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was on the very next day that Zeljko told me that the two of us had to go; that is to say, that Dule Jankovic had ordered him that the two of us should report to Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that same day when he told me this, he said that he had some business to attend to and that we would go in a few hours time. That is what happened. We went and found Dusan Jankovic in his office in the building of the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the conversation that you had with Jankovic and was Mr. Meakic present?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zeljko was present. Jankovic just said very briefly, "Kvocka, where are your brothers-in-law?" I answered, "They're at my place, at my house with my parents." He said, "Go back and take them to the investigating centre and report to me tomorrow morning here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back home. I said that this was something we had to do because the situation was highly volatile. The three of them got into the car with me, and I drove them back to the investigate centre. I found there the duty officer who was Momcilo Gruban, who gave me the impression of being a decent and honest man. I said to him, "Here you are. Take care of them if you can. Help them, and I will probably come to visit them occasionally."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was this the last day of your service in the Omarska police station department and, thereby, also in the mining compound of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening when I left them there and went back home, that was my last day of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been the 22nd or 23rd of June 1992. Taking into account the day when I had to report to Jankovic that morning, then that must be the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your status in the ensuing days and what were your activities? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning, as he said, I reported, but he wasn't there or, rather, his secretary said he was busy and that I should wait for a while and we'd see. However, he didn't turn up that day. So I came back the next day, and for another day I called up the secretary by phone from my apartment to tell me whether Dule Jankovic could see me. Eventually this did happen. One day towards the end of June, again we had a brief conversation. All he said to me was, "Go to the reserve police force in a locality called Tukovi, a suburb of Prijedor, in the direction of Sanski Most, and report to Mile Drazic there, who is the commander there. You will assist them in their work."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, allow me now to read a document which has already been tendered, D13/1, that is exhibit number. It was our document DP8. Allow me to read item 1 of the letter of the 12th of March 1993, signed by the head of the centre, Marko Dzenadija: "Kvocka Miroslav worked in Omarska including the 23rd of June 1993, when he terminated his employment and went on a seven-day leave to end on the 30th of June inclusive, Omarska." The text is now on the monitor. Paragraph 2 of this letter reads, "The policeman Kvocka Miroslav worked in Omarska until June 23rd, 1992, when he handed over the duty and took a seven-day leave ending June 30th, 1992, when he came back to work in the Tukovi police station." This is paragraph 1. I'm sorry. Can this official report be accepted as correct, the report being issued by the public security centre in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this fits, only I see that they registered me as if I had been on leave because that is what I had asked Jankovic to do. But it wasn't really a vacation. It couldn't have been a vacation for me. I was thinking whether I would be fired or be put in prison or who knows what else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't deal in detail with the Tukovi police station because it is outside the relevant issues, but we will introduce evidence to show that you did begin working there, because according to the Prosecution, your responsibility ends with the 30th of June. But Mr. Niemann, in his opening statement, again referred to the whole period. So we wonder now whether we need to prove the fact that Mr. Kvocka really did, on the 1st of July 1992, begin working in the Tukovi police station. According to the amended indictment, there would be no need to introduce evidence to prove this, but in view of the opening statement by my learned friend Mr. Niemann, we would need to prove that fact. When you arrived at the Omarska police station, who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Omarska or Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No. I'm sorry. Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Mile Drazic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the reserve or active-duty policemen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His deputy was Slavko Antonic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Antonic. Where was he working and what was his status, active duty or reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Antonic was also a reserve policeman, and he used to work in the economy, I think, in the post office in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the assistant commander of the Tukovi police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Lazar Basrak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his status?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basrak was an active-duty policeman who came after the well-known events in Croatia. He had to leave Zagreb. But I think that at the time in the Tukovi station, he still didn't have any official decision as an active-duty policeman. So one could really describe him as being a reserve policeman. But by occupation, he was a professional policeman. I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Basak's situation later on, three or four years later? Did he get employment in the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He started working later in the public security station in Prijedor for a number of years, 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996. I think he stayed on working there after I was arrested in the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your duty in the Tukovi police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no specific assignments in Tukovi except to be on duty in a small auxiliary office which was part of the premises of the local community, and I would assist Mile Drazic with the administrative work, because he was not qualified for these administrative duties. So I usually was on duty there, then I'd go home when I was off duty, and then I'd come back again to Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, during your stay in Tukovi -- let me rephrase that. What was the attitude of the superiors in the Tukovi police station towards you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any outspoken problems, but everyone was very reserved towards me. Basrak would exchange a few words with me occasionally about policing since he had spent many years in Zagreb as a policeman, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you go on working in the Tukovi police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it difficult to recall exactly, but it could have been until sometime in September when I stopped working in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason for your stopping to work in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was talk already then about the termination and the closure of that police station, but a couple of days before that, several of us from Tukovi were assigned to provide security for a gathering in Prijedor. After I participated in providing security, I no longer worked in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this gathering?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an assembly, a joint-assembly meeting of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was a rather important gathering in those days and quite a number of policemen provided the security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty was to stand on one corner of the hotel, and should any person try to do something in that area, to attack the hotel in any way, it was my duty to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which hotel was this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Prijedor Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in the centre of town or is it on the bank of the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a hotel on the Sana River, right close to the bridge there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, roughly, to end this story about Tukovi, how many days went by from the security of that event to the disbanding of the station in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a long period of time, but I don't know exactly. It could be 15 -- I could say 15 and it could be 25, so I wouldn't be precise in giving an estimate. Since I never went back to Tukovi after that, I lost interest in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought that the examination would take three, maybe four days. It seems that it will have to take a fourth day. We have ended one subject area. Perhaps it would not be good to embark upon another subject area now. But of course, I am at your disposal regarding what you think we should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, Mr. Simic, you need another day at least to complete the testimony of Mr. Kvocka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half a day. Roughly. I have a couple of more subject areas, meals, medical treatment, and that would be more or less the end. About half a day, according to my judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Simic. Let me ask Mr. Fila. Are you ready to begin on Monday, following the end of this examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm ready to begin on Monday, but it depends on when Mr. Krstan Simic finishes his part of the work. What I promised you and the Prosecution is that it will be very brief if we agree that Mr. Radic accepts everything that Mr. Kvocka has said so that I don't have to go through it again to ask Radic, "Where is Prijedor? Where is Omarska?" and all these things all over again. I don't think that is necessary. It will be too tiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Fila. I think it is better for us to adjourn for the moment and to embark upon your next subject on Monday. As soon as Mr. Kvocka finishes his testimony, we will begin with the testimony of Mr. Radic on Monday. So for today, that will be all. As you know, we have no hearing tomorrow, so I wish you success in your work and a pleasant weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
